Acceptance summary:

This is an exciting paper demonstrating roles for cortical astrocytes in sleep. Activity in networks of neurons throughout the brain is different when an animal is asleep compared to when it is awake, and it has long been speculated that astrocytes, non-neuronal cells in the brain, may be partly responsible for regulating neuronal network activity during sleep. However, solid evidence has been largely lacking until recently. This paper plays an important in elucidating the connection between astrocytes and sleep, and suggests that astrocytes play a homeostatic role in regulating neurons during sleep.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Cortical astrocytes independently regulate sleep depth and duration via separate GPCR pathways" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Laura Colgin as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

We would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). Specifically, when editors judge that a submitted work as a whole belongs in eLife but that some conclusions require a modest amount of additional new data, as they do with your paper, we are asking that the manuscript be revised to either limit claims to those supported by data in hand, or to explicitly state that the relevant conclusions require additional supporting data.

Our expectation is that the authors will eventually carry out the additional experiments and report on how they affect the relevant conclusions either in a preprint on bioRxiv or medRxiv, or if appropriate, as a Research Advance in eLife, either of which would be linked to the original paper.

Summary

This work builds on several recent publications implicating astrocyte control of sleep but represents an several new findings that provide new insight toward elucidating the mechanisms underlying the reported observations. The paper presents high quality data, rigorous experiments and analyses. Overall the paper is well written; however, there are several (relatively straightforward) points to address prior to publication as summarized below from both reviewers.

Revisions for this paper:

– Please revise to increase clarity in text and figures as suggested.

– The temporal relationships between astrocyte signals and SWA changes is complex, with SWA decreasing before astrocyte calcium events and increasing after. This is interpreted as astrocytes having a homeostatic effect on SWA. Causality is therefore somewhat hard to interpret, in part because the homeostatic effect may involve more than just astrocytes but also neurons or other cell types. Including imaging data of cortical astrocytes together with nearby cortical neurons could help clarify the temporal relationship between these cells. If this data is not available, please address this possibility.

– Along similar lines, the authors demonstrate sufficiency, but do not conclusively demonstrate that sleep is regulated through these pathways because of the difficulty in knocking them out. Please temper claims and address alternative interpretations in the Discussion.

– Is CNO is equally efficacious at Gi and Gq DREADDs for downstream signaling in astrocytes? Please comment or determine if the Gi and Gq DREADDs are expressed to the same level in astrocytes (see points 3,4 reviewer #1 and related comments by reviewer 2).

– In this study SWA, measured through LFP, is used as the primary measure of sleep; however SWA can also be measured from EEG, a more common way to define sleep states. Can data be included that quantifies the degree to which these are correlated? Other indicators of sleep include arousal threshold could also help show relationships between their LFP-measure of SWA and such other measures? Please include or address potential caveats in paper if data cannot be included.

Reviewer #1:

The paper by Poskanzer and colleagues presents a detailed description of astrocyte calcium dynamics during natural sleep and then explores the consequences on slow wave activity (SWA) of stimulating astrocyte Gi and Gq DREADDs. Overall, this study builds on several years' worth of work by many labs showing or at least suggesting potentially important roles of astrocytes in sleep. As such, the topic and the data are not completely novel, but to their credit the authors have performed in depth analyses that go far deeper than previous studies. The depth of the analyses and the rigor of the approach outweigh any concerns that may linger regarding past work and push this study into a category of paper that is much needed and valued in the field. Seems highly appropriate for eLife.

No major concerns.

Reviewer #2:

This is an exciting paper showing relationships between sleep and Gi- and Gq-coupled GPCR signaling pathways in astrocytes. The paper demonstrates correlations between astrocyte calcium signals and sleep signatures such as slow-wave activity (SWA) measured with LFP in cortex. Astrocytes show activity changes near SWA changes such as at sleep-wake transitions. These are investigated using Gi- and Gq-DREADDs and it is found that astrocytes have a causal effect on SWA and the frequency of sleep-wake transitions. These results provide evidence for a role for astrocytes in controlling sleep-related SWA, with separate effects on sleep depth and duration depending on which GPCR pathway is perturbed.

This work is related to other recent publications implicating astrocyte control of sleep and contains a multitude of new findings. These are very interesting and elucidating while also pointing toward directions of research needed for determining the molecular and mechanisms underlying the reported observations.

1) The conclusions are somewhat indirect when it comes to causal relationships and mechanisms. The temporal relationships between astrocyte signals and SWA changes is complex, with SWA decreasing before astrocyte calcium events and increasing after. This is interpreted as astrocytes having a homeostatic effect on SWA. Causality is therefore somewhat hard to interpret, in part because the homeostatic effect may involve more than just astrocytes but also neurons, including neurons whose activity is less visible in LFP measurements of SWA. Although this may be outside the scope of this study, if the authors have imaging data available of cortical astrocytes together with nearby cortical neurons (that is, a more direct measure of nearby neuron activity than LFP), this might clarify the temporal relationship between these cells.

2) The paper demonstrates sufficiency, astrocytes can change cortical SWA and sleep duration, but does not conclusively demonstrate that sleep is regulated through these pathways in natural behavior because of the difficulty in knocking them out. Can the text (perhaps the title) be adjusted to reflect this?

3) The authors show that there is inverse relationship between SWA amplitude and astrocytic calcium events in Figure 1H, with higher calcium activities associated with lower SWA. Gi-DREADD activation by CNO can increase astrocytic calcium events, and also increase SWA. Can the authors discuss this changed relationship in more depth? In addition, Gq-DREADD can change sleep time and sleep-wake transition, but not change SWA. Do these results indicate that astrocytic calcium may be not directly affect sleep duration or depth, but some other signal downstream of the GPCR?

4) In the Gi-DREADD experiments, the IP3R2-/- mouse is tested and found to lead to a smaller effect of CNO on SWA. Why was the IP3R2-/- not included in the Gq-DREADD experiments? Was that based on the assumption that there would be no difference, since Ca events disappeared in the Gq experiments?

5) It is unclear what the true effect of the Gq-DREADDs is on astrocyte calcium because activity is only represented by event rate (extracted by AQuA) and not as Ca concentration. Does event rate go down because Ca concentration drops to low levels and shows no dynamics, or because Ca concentration saturates and shows no dynamics due to a ceiling effect (as in the wake cocktail experiments)? This could be measured as absolute fluorescence of GCaMP. Interpretation of the results could change depending on which one of these is true. For example, saturated calcium could indicate an “unphysiological” state of astrocytes that can have consequences on the network that may not occur during natural sleep/wake.

6) The conclusion that "Gq-induced Ca2+ is necessary for sleep-wake transitions" (text and Figure 6) seems somewhat overstated. The Gq-DREADDs are a useful way to perturb calcium dynamics and this leads to changes in sleep-wake transitions, but it was not shown that without Gq sleep-wake transitions disappear. Also the effect demonstrated (Figure 6F for example) is partial. It seems appropriate to rephrase this statement.

7) SWA, measured through LFP, is used as the primary measure of sleep. SWA can also be measured from EEG, and this appears the more common way to define sleep states. Can data be included that quantifies the degree to which these are correlated? Is cortical LFP-measured SWA one hundred percent predictive of SWA derived from EEG? Other indicators of sleep include arousal threshold. Do the authors have data showing relationships between their LFP-measure of SWA and such other measures?

8) Related to this, how are changes in LFP-measured SWA in local cortical areas related to EEG-measured SWA during perturbation experiments? This is partially addressed in Figure 7 by measuring SWA with LFP in another cortical area, but it would be interesting to compare this to a global EEG measure.

9) Is there any possibility that manipulation of astrocytes may directly influence LFP, for example through secretion of ions? It seems unlikely, but not impossible.

results.result: Endogenous astrocyte Ca2+ event rate is inversely correlated with slow-wave activity (SWA) across behavioral states. Ca2+ event rate is highest during locomotory wake, lower during stationary wake, and lowest during sleep, while SWA shows the opposite pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C16, C23, C24, C25, and C30 collectively demonstrate a robust negative correlation between astrocyte Ca2+ event rate and SWA across multiple behavioral states, supported by statistical analysis (Pearson's correlation, p<0.0005) and consistent patterns across different experimental conditions (Figure 1D, F, G, H).

results.result: Astrocyte Ca2+ events exhibit unique spatiotemporal signatures across behavioral states when multiple features are analyzed together using principal component analysis, despite no individual feature differences between sleep and stationary wake.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C29 demonstrate that while individual Ca2+ event features (size, duration, amplitude) do not differ between sleep and stationary wake when analyzed separately (C27), PCA incorporating 20 event features reveals significant differences across all five principal components examined (C28), supported by two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

results.result: The relationship between astrocyte Ca2+ event rate and SWA is partially dependent on IP3R2, with the most dramatic change in correlation observed during sleep in IP3R2 KO mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C32, and C35 demonstrate that IP3R2 KO mice show decreased correlation between Ca2+ and SWA (Figure 1I) and reduced SWA modulation around Ca2+ events (Figure 2C-D), with the most pronounced effect during sleep, indicating partial IP3R2 dependence of the astrocyte-SWA relationship.

results.result: Astrocyte Ca2+ events are preceded by decreases in SWA and followed by increases in SWA, with significantly higher modulation during sleep compared to stationary wake.
results.evaluation: Claims C33 and C34 are supported by Ca2+ event-triggered averages showing consistent temporal patterns of SWA modulation around Ca2+ events (Figure 2C), with statistical confirmation that modulation is significantly higher during sleep (Figure 2D, rank sum test).

results.result: Gi-DREADD activation in astrocytes increases Ca2+ event frequency and SWA during sleep without affecting sleep duration or wake SWA, and these effects are dependent on IP3R2.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C41 and C92 collectively demonstrate that Gi-DREADD activation increases astrocyte Ca2+ (Figure 3C-D) and sleep SWA (Figure 3E) via IP3R2-dependent mechanisms (Figure 3I-J), while not affecting sleep duration (Figure 3F, H) or wake SWA (Figure 3G). Control experiments confirm CNO alone has no effect (C92, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

results.result: Gi-DREADD activation in astrocytes preferentially increases SWA by enhancing delta wave amplitude more than slow oscillation amplitude, without changing the rate of either waveform type.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C47 demonstrate that Gi-DREADD activation does not change delta wave or slow oscillation rates (C43, Figure 4E) but significantly increases peak-trough amplitude for both waveforms, with delta waves showing significantly greater changes than slow oscillations (C46, Figure 4L), supported by paired t-tests and cumulative distribution analyses.

results.result: Astrocyte Ca2+ event rate exhibits bidirectional changes preceding sleep-wake transitions, with increases before sleep-to-wake transitions and decreases before wake-to-sleep transitions, and these changes are abolished in IP3R2 KO mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 demonstrate consistent bidirectional Ca2+ dynamics preceding state transitions (Figure 5A), with quantitative confirmation that event rate increases in the last third of sleep and decreases in the last third of wake (C49, Figure 5D), and that these patterns are abolished in IP3R2 KO mice (C50-C51, Figure 5B, D).

results.result: Gq-DREADD activation in astrocytes produces a brief initial increase in Ca2+ (5-10 minutes) followed by near-complete suppression of Ca2+ activity lasting 2-3 hours, across all tested CNO concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 and C85 describe an unexpected biphasic response to Gq-DREADD activation, with initial Ca2+ increase followed by ~97% suppression (Figure 6C-D), consistent across multiple CNO doses (0.1-1 mg/kg, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F-H), representing a novel finding about Gq-DREADD effects in awake astrocytes.

results.result: During the Ca2+ suppression period following Gq-DREADD activation, mice spend more time in sleep and make fewer sleep-to-wake and wake-to-sleep transitions, without changes in SWA.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 and C71 demonstrate that Gq-DREADD-induced Ca2+ suppression increases sleep time (Figure 6E) and decreases both sleep-to-wake and wake-to-sleep transitions (Figure 6F), while not affecting SWA (C59, Figure 6H), supported by paired t-tests across 11 mice.

results.result: During the initial high Ca2+ period after Gq-DREADD activation, mice show decreased sleep time compared to saline controls.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 is based on a small subset of animals (n=4) that exhibited sleep during the brief initial high Ca2+ period (Figure 6G). While statistically significant, the limited sample size and short duration of this period make this finding less robust than other results in the study.

results.result: V1-FC coherence (5-10 Hz) is higher immediately following astrocyte Ca2+ events, and astrocyte event-locked coherence (0-15 Hz) increases in the 15 seconds prior to sleep-to-wake transitions.
results.evaluation: Claims C60 and C61 demonstrate increased inter-cortical coherence associated with astrocyte Ca2+ events (Figure 7D, paired t-test with Bonferroni correction) and preceding state transitions (Figure 7E, unpaired t-test), suggesting astrocytes may coordinate activity across distant cortical regions.

results.result: Gi-DREADD activation in V1 astrocytes increases SWA in contralateral frontal cortex through selective enhancement of slow oscillation amplitude, with similar magnitude changes in V1 and FC slow oscillations.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C65 demonstrate that local V1 astrocyte activation produces remote effects in FC, with significant SWA increases (Figure 7F-H) driven by slow oscillation amplitude changes (Figure 7I-J), and similar magnitude changes in V1 (8.8±3.2%) and FC (6.8±2.2%) slow oscillations (C64), suggesting propagation of slow oscillations across cortex.

results.result: Astrocytic Gi- and Gq-coupled GPCR signaling separately control NREM sleep depth and duration, respectively, with Gi-GPCR-induced Ca2+ sufficient to increase SWA and Gq-GPCR signaling necessary for sleep-wake transitions.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C18, C19, C66-C68, and C70 represent the central finding of the manuscript, demonstrating functional dissociation between Gi- and Gq-GPCR pathways in astrocytes. This is supported by comprehensive experimental evidence showing Gi-DREADD increases SWA without affecting sleep duration (Figures 3E-F), while Gq-DREADD manipulation affects sleep duration and transitions without changing SWA (Figures 6E-F, 6H).

results.result: Astrocytic signaling causes differential changes in local versus remote cortex, with local V1 changes driven by delta waves and remote FC changes driven by slow oscillations.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C20-C22, and C69 demonstrate spatial specificity of astrocyte effects, with local V1 manipulation preferentially affecting delta waves (Figure 4) while remote FC shows selective slow oscillation changes (Figure 7I-J), supported by paired t-tests and immunohistochemistry confirming restricted viral expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

results.result: Endogenous astrocyte Ca2+ is modulated in relation to both sleep duration and sleep depth, but Gi-DREADD experiments suggest SWA does not directly influence sleep duration.
results.evaluation: Claims C72 and C73 synthesize findings showing astrocyte Ca2+ correlates with both SWA (Figure 1) and precedes state transitions (Figure 5), yet Gi-DREADD can increase SWA without affecting sleep duration (Figure 3E-F), suggesting these regulatory mechanisms can be dissociated despite endogenous coupling.

results.result: Both Gi- and Gq-GPCRs increase intracellular Ca2+ in astrocytes, yet there is functional dissociation between these pathways, suggesting astrocytes interpret Ca2+ dynamics differently depending on GPCR signaling context.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C83 synthesize the key mechanistic insight that despite both GPCR types increasing Ca2+ (supported by citations and experimental data), they produce distinct functional outcomes (sleep depth vs. duration), suggesting Ca2+ is not the sole determinant of astrocyte function but rather GPCR-specific signaling cascades are critical. However, C82-C83 involve some speculation about parallel functions.

results.result: Background claims establishing that NREM sleep is characterized by SWA and serves critical functions, that sleep depth and duration can be independently controlled, and that astrocytes express GPCRs responsive to neuromodulators and regulate SWA under anesthesia.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C15 represent established knowledge from prior literature, supported by multiple citations throughout the introduction. These provide the scientific foundation and rationale for the current study but are not novel findings from this work.

results.result: Additional background claims from the discussion citing prior work on astrocyte Ca2+ changes with circadian rhythm and sleep deprivation, roles of GABA and glutamate in sleep, astrocyte receptor expression, and delta wave/slow oscillation characteristics.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C79, C84, C86, C88-C89, C91, and C93 represent established findings from prior literature cited in the discussion to contextualize the current results. These are appropriately cited and provide important context but are not novel findings from this manuscript.

results.result: Methodological details describing the IP3R2 KO mouse model, recording time windows (ZT 2-5), use of AQuA software for Ca2+ event detection, and criteria for sleep scoring and waveform detection.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C99 describe methodological approaches used in the study. These are clearly documented in the Materials and methods section and are essential for reproducibility, but represent technical details rather than scientific findings.

results.result: Endogenous astrocyte Ca2+ activity is inversely correlated with slow-wave activity (SWA) across behavioral states, with Ca2+ event rate highest during locomotory wake, lower during stationary wake, and lowest during sleep. This relationship is partially dependent on IP3R2, as IP3R2 KO mice show decreased correlation between Ca2+ and SWA, particularly during sleep.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'no major concerns' and Reviewer 2 describes the paper as 'exciting' with 'high quality data, rigorous experiments and analyses.' The correlational findings between astrocyte Ca2+ and SWA are not questioned by reviewers, indicating acceptance of these observational results.

results.result: Astrocyte Ca2+ events show distinct spatial, temporal, and amplitude signatures across behavioral states. While individual event features (size, duration, amplitude) do not differ between sleep and stationary wake when compared individually, principal component analysis reveals significant differences across all five principal components when multiple features are incorporated.
results.evaluation: These detailed characterization findings are part of the 'in depth analyses that go far deeper than previous studies' praised by Reviewer 1. No concerns are raised about the PCA methodology or conclusions, suggesting reviewer acceptance of these analytical results.

results.result: Ca2+ events are preceded by decreases in SWA and followed by increases in SWA during sleep and stationary wake, with this modulation significantly higher during sleep. This SWA modulation around Ca2+ events is decreased in IP3R2 KO mice, indicating partial dependence on IP3R2.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'the temporal relationships between astrocyte signals and SWA changes is complex' and states 'causality is therefore somewhat hard to interpret, in part because the homeostatic effect may involve more than just astrocytes but also neurons or other cell types.' The reviewer requests additional data with neurons if available, indicating uncertainty about the mechanistic interpretation despite accepting the temporal observations.

results.result: Gi-DREADD activation in astrocytes increases Ca2+ event frequency and significantly increases SWA during sleep without affecting total time spent in sleep/wake or SWA during wake. These effects are dependent on IP3R2, as IP3R2 KO mice show no significant changes in Ca2+ or SWA with CNO administration.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes an apparent contradiction: 'there is inverse relationship between SWA amplitude and astrocytic calcium events in Figure 1H, with higher calcium activities associated with lower SWA. Gi-DREADD activation by CNO can increase astrocytic calcium events, and also increase SWA. Can the authors discuss this changed relationship in more depth?' This indicates uncertainty about the mechanistic interpretation. Additionally, Reviewer 2 states 'the paper demonstrates sufficiency, astrocytes can change cortical SWA and sleep duration, but does not conclusively demonstrate that sleep is regulated through these pathways in natural behavior' and requests tempering of claims.

results.result: Gi-DREADD activation does not change the rate of delta waves or slow oscillations but increases their amplitude, with delta wave amplitude changes significantly higher than slow oscillation changes. This demonstrates that astrocyte Ca2+ through Gi-GPCR signaling preferentially increases SWA by altering delta wave amplitude.
results.evaluation: These findings are part of the detailed mechanistic analysis praised by reviewers. Reviewer 1 notes 'the depth of the analyses and the rigor of the approach' as strengths. No specific concerns are raised about the delta wave versus slow oscillation analysis, indicating acceptance of these results.

results.result: Ca2+ event rate exhibits bidirectional changes prior to sleep-wake transitions, increasing in the last third of sleep before sleep-to-wake transitions and decreasing in the last third of wake before wake-to-sleep transitions. These changes are abolished in IP3R2 KO mice.
results.evaluation: While reviewers note complexity in temporal relationships generally, these specific findings about Ca2+ dynamics preceding transitions are not directly challenged. The IP3R2 KO validation strengthens the conclusions. Reviewer 1 has 'no major concerns' about the overall findings.

results.result: Gq-DREADD activation causes a brief initial increase in Ca2+ (5-10 min) followed by almost complete suppression of Ca2+ dynamics for 2-3 hours. During this Ca2+ suppression period, mice spent significantly more time in sleep and made fewer sleep-to-wake and wake-to-sleep transitions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises critical questions: 'It is unclear what the true effect of the Gq-DREADDs is on astrocyte calcium because activity is only represented by event rate (extracted by AQuA) and not as Ca concentration. Does event rate go down because Ca concentration drops to low levels and shows no dynamics, or because Ca concentration saturates and shows no dynamics due to a ceiling effect?' The reviewer notes 'interpretation of the results could change depending on which one of these is true.' Additionally, Reviewer 2 states the conclusion about Gq being 'necessary' is 'somewhat overstated' since 'it was not shown that without Gq sleep-wake transitions disappear' and 'the effect demonstrated...is partial.'

results.result: During the initial high Ca2+ period after CNO administration in Gq-DREADD mice, there was a significant decrease in percent time sleeping.
results.evaluation: This finding is presented as part of the Gq-DREADD characterization. While reviewers question the interpretation of the Ca2+ suppression phase, this initial effect observation is not specifically challenged.

results.result: Ca2+ suppression via Gq-GPCR manipulation had no significant effect on SWA during sleep, in contrast to Gi-GPCR manipulation.
results.evaluation: This differential effect between Gi and Gq pathways is a key finding that reviewers do not challenge. The dissociation between the two pathways is part of what makes the study novel and is implicitly accepted by reviewers' overall positive assessment.

results.result: V1-FC coherence (5-10 Hz) is higher immediately following astrocyte Ca2+ events compared to randomly chosen epochs, and astrocyte event-locked coherence (0-15 Hz) increases in the 15 seconds prior to sleep-to-wake transitions.
results.evaluation: These coherence findings support the cortex-wide effects of astrocytes. Reviewers do not raise specific concerns about these measurements, and they fit within the overall framework of the study that reviewers find rigorous.

results.result: Increasing Ca2+ via Gi-DREADDs in V1 increases SWA in contralateral frontal cortex (though less than in V1), with this increase accounted for by slow oscillation amplitude changes rather than delta waves. The similar magnitude of slow oscillation changes in V1 and FC suggests slow oscillations travel between regions, demonstrating cortex-wide astrocyte influence.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'this is partially addressed in Figure 7 by measuring SWA with LFP in another cortical area' and asks about comparison to 'global EEG measure,' suggesting interest in extending rather than challenging these findings. The cortex-wide effects are part of the novel contributions that make the paper 'exciting' according to reviewers.

results.result: CNO itself (1 mg/kg, I.P.) did not alter Ca2+ dynamics or sleep features in the absence of DREADD expression.
results.evaluation: This control experiment addresses potential confounds. Reviewers do not question this control, and it represents good experimental practice that aligns with the 'rigorous experiments' praised by reviewers.

results.result: Cortical astrocytes regulate distinct features of sleep via differential GPCR signaling: Gi-GPCR signaling controls sleep depth (SWA) through delta wave enhancement, while Gq-GPCR signaling controls sleep duration through regulation of sleep-wake transitions. This represents a functional dissociation between the two GPCR pathways despite both increasing intracellular Ca2+.
results.evaluation: This is the central claim of the paper. While reviewers find the work 'exciting' and praise the data quality, Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'the paper demonstrates sufficiency, astrocytes can change cortical SWA and sleep duration, but does not conclusively demonstrate that sleep is regulated through these pathways in natural behavior because of the difficulty in knocking them out. Can the text (perhaps the title) be adjusted to reflect this?' This indicates the sufficiency is demonstrated but necessity is not, requiring more cautious claims. Additionally, questions about CNO efficacy at Gi vs Gq DREADDs and expression levels remain unaddressed.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the negative correlation between astrocyte Ca2+ event rate and SWA (C16, C23, C24, C25, C30). OpenEval finds these claims SUPPORTED with robust statistical evidence. Peer reviewers also find these correlational findings SUPPORTED, with no major concerns raised about the observational results. Peer R1 additionally includes C31-C32 (IP3R2 KO effects).

Peer reviewers praise these as part of 'in depth analyses that go far deeper than previous studies' with no concerns about the PCA methodology or conclusions.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting an apparent contradiction between inverse Ca2+-SWA relationship in Figure 1H versus Gi-DREADD increasing both, and stating the paper 'demonstrates sufficiency' but not that 'sleep is regulated through these pathways in natural behavior.' Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, noting these findings are part of detailed mechanistic analysis praised for 'depth of analyses and rigor of approach' with no specific concerns raised. Peer R5 also includes C87.

Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, noting that while temporal relationships are complex generally, these specific findings are not directly challenged and IP3R2 KO strengthens conclusions. Peer R6 also includes C17.

Peer R7 rates UNCERTAIN, raising critical questions about whether event rate decrease reflects low Ca2+ concentration or ceiling effect saturation, noting 'interpretation of the results could change' depending on which is true. Peer R7 also includes C55-C57, C71.

OpenEval R9 addresses Gq-DREADD effects on sleep time and transitions (C55-C57, C71) and finds them SUPPORTED. Peer R7 covers overlapping claims but rates UNCERTAIN, questioning the Ca2+ measurement interpretation and noting the conclusion about Gq being 'necessary' is 'somewhat overstated' since 'the effect demonstrated...is partial.' Peer R7 also includes C52-C54.

OpenEval R9 addresses lack of SWA effect with Gq-DREADD (C58). Peer R9 evaluates C59 (same differential effect concept) as SUPPORTED, noting this dissociation between Gi and Gq pathways is a key finding that makes the study novel and is implicitly accepted by reviewers.

Perfect match on C58 regarding initial high Ca2+ period SWA increase. OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to small sample size (n=4) and brief duration. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, noting this initial effect observation is not specifically challenged though they question interpretation of the subsequent Ca2+ suppression phase.

Perfect match on inter-cortical coherence findings (C60, C61). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers find these claims SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note these measurements fit within the overall rigorous framework and support cortex-wide effects of astrocytes without raising specific concerns.

Both evaluate remote cortical effects of local V1 astrocyte activation (C62-C65). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 2 noting interest in extending rather than challenging these findings, and considering cortex-wide effects as part of novel contributions making the paper 'exciting.' Peer R11 also includes C20, C22.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, explicitly stating the paper 'demonstrates sufficiency' but 'does not conclusively demonstrate that sleep is regulated through these pathways in natural behavior,' requesting adjusted claims. Peer R13 also includes C81; OpenEval R13 includes C18, C19, C70.
